title: MYP Physical and Health Education Revision Plan
summary: MYP Physical and Health Education revision made practical. Learn what to practise, assess work against criteria, build evidence, and manage your time calmly.
body_markdown:
MYP Physical and Health Education revision is not mainly about memorising fitness definitions the night before an examination. For eAssessment, Physical and Health Education is assessed through an ePortfolio. You need to show how you understand performance, plan improvement, apply physical skills and reflect on what happened.


That changes the preparation strategy. A strong student does not simply train harder or write more. They collect purposeful evidence, connect decisions to the assessment criteria and leave enough time to improve before recording their final performance.


The practical plan is simple: understand the task, establish a baseline, choose a precise target, create and follow a justified plan, record progress, evaluate the final performance and check every section against the relevant descriptors. The details of the task can vary, so always follow the current instructions and unit materials supplied by your school.


### Your preparation checklist


Before starting, make sure you can answer these questions:


- What performance or activity is being assessed?
- What evidence must be included in the ePortfolio?
- Which sections address criteria A, B, C and D?
- What is your starting level, and how will you demonstrate it?
- What physical and psychological performance target will you pursue?
- How will you measure progress rather than merely describe effort?
- When will you record your final performance?
- How much time will remain for reflection, editing and technical checks?


If any answer is uncertain, ask your teacher early. Ten minutes of clarification can prevent several hours of producing evidence that does not answer the task.


For broader context, read RevisionDojo’s guides to[MYP Physical and Health Education objectives and skills](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/physical-and-health-education-objectives-and-skills-in-myp) and[the eight MYP subject groups](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-subjects-are-taught-in-myp) .


### Understand what the PHE eAssessment requires


Physical and Health Education does not use the same assessment format as MYP subjects with on-screen examinations. It uses an ePortfolio, marked by the student’s teacher against published Year 5 criteria, with samples moderated by IB examiners to support consistent international standards. RevisionDojo’s explanation of[which MYP subjects have eAssessment](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-subjects-have-myp-eassessment) helps clarify this distinction.


The four equally weighted criteria are:


- **Criterion A: Knowing and understanding**
- **Criterion B: Planning for performance**
- **Criterion C: Applying and performing**
- **Criterion D: Reflecting and improving performance**


Each criterion has a maximum achievement level of 8. This matters because excellent physical ability alone cannot carry the entire portfolio. A polished reflection cannot replace weak performance evidence either. The ePortfolio rewards a connected process in which knowledge informs planning, planning shapes action and evidence supports reflection.


Read the current task instructions before using generic advice. The required activity, evidence and response structure can change between tasks and sessions. Your teacher’s instructions and the materials issued for your assessment are therefore your operational source of truth.


### What to practise for MYP Physical and Health Education


### Establish a useful baseline


Your initial performance should reveal something worth improving. Record evidence that lets you identify strengths and limitations. Depending on the activity, useful measures might include accuracy, successful decisions, consistency, movement quality, completion time or a relevant fitness indicator.


Choose measures that match the performance. Counting successful passes may be useful in one activity, while evaluating rhythm, control and transitions may be more appropriate in another. A number is not automatically better than an observation. The best evidence is evidence that helps you make a decision.


### Build technical and tactical skill


Separate your practice into smaller components. A student working on a game performance might isolate technique, movement off the ball and decision-making before combining them in a realistic situation. A student preparing a routine might practise individual movements, transitions, timing and expressive quality separately.


Use a simple cycle:


1. Perform the skill under controlled conditions.
2. Review a recording or obtain focused feedback.
3. Identify one specific adjustment.
4. Repeat the skill with that adjustment.
5. Test it in a more realistic performance context.


This is better than repeating the same movement without changing anything. Repetition preserves whatever you repeat, including errors.


### Practise the thinking around performance


PHE also requires knowledge and explanation. You may need to apply principles connected to training, health, strategy, movement or psychological preparation. Build concise RevisionDojo **Flashcards** for terminology, then use **Study Notes** and the **Questionbank** to practise applying ideas rather than only recalling definitions.


For instance, knowing what a training principle means is the beginning. Explaining why it suits your target, how you applied it and what evidence suggests it worked is the more valuable skill. **AI Chat** can help you question an unclear concept, while **Tutors** can challenge the reasoning behind your plan.


Two students discover that organising files is not a substitute for practising the sport


*An immaculate folder helps, but performance still has to happen.*


### Use the criteria to self-assess


Criteria become useful when you turn them from labels into questions. Before submitting a section, read the exact descriptor supplied by your teacher and highlight its command terms. Words such as *identify* , *describe* , *explain* , *analyse* , *evaluate* and *justify* demand different depths of response.


### Check criterion A


Ask whether your knowledge is accurate, relevant and applied to the problem. Do not insert every fact you know about fitness or health. Select concepts that explain your decisions and connect them directly to performance.


### Check criterion B


Your plan should follow logically from your baseline and target. Check whether the target is specific enough to evaluate, whether the activities address the identified weakness and whether the plan considers both physical and psychological dimensions where required.


A timetable is not automatically a good plan. Explain why the frequency, sequence, duration and methods are suitable. RevisionDojo’s[guide to the MYP ePortfolio](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-eportfolio) provides useful context for connecting process evidence to assessment.


### Check criterion C


Criterion C concerns what you can apply and perform. Make sure recordings show the relevant skills clearly and under appropriate conditions. Evidence should allow a viewer to judge control, technique, strategy, movement concepts or other features relevant to the task.


Do not rely on editing to create the impression of quality. Select evidence that represents your performance honestly and check practical details such as visibility, framing, sound and file accessibility.


### Check criterion D


Reflection should explain what changed, why it changed and what the evidence suggests. Compare the final performance with the baseline and target. Discuss strengths as well as limitations, then propose improvements that follow from the evidence.


A useful structure is: claim, evidence, interpretation and next action. “My accuracy improved” is a claim. The relevant performance data or observed change is evidence. Explaining why your practice contributed is interpretation. Identifying the next adjustment completes the reflection.


RevisionDojo’s **Grading tools** can help you test whether written analysis addresses a criterion, while the **Coursework Library** can show how strong academic structure differs from unsupported description. Use examples to understand quality, never to copy another student’s work.


### Manage your time without rushing the evidence


The hardest deadline is often not submission day. It is the last realistic opportunity to improve your performance before recording it.


Work backwards from the school deadline:


- **Planning phase:** understand the task, collect baseline evidence and create the target.
- **Development phase:** follow the plan, record progress and make justified adjustments.
- **Performance phase:** capture the final performance while time remains for a second recording if permitted and necessary.
- **Reflection phase:** compare evidence, evaluate the plan and explain personal growth.
- **Quality-control phase:** check criteria, citations, filenames, permissions, file formats and playback.


Protect short weekly review sessions rather than leaving the written work until the end. After each practical session, spend 10-15 minutes recording what happened, what evidence you collected and what you will change next. Contemporary notes are usually more precise than memories reconstructed several weeks later.


RevisionDojo’s broader guide to[MYP eAssessment preparation platforms](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/study-platforms-myp-eassessment-prep) can help you organise digital preparation. **Predicted Papers** and **Mock Exams** are valuable for on-screen MYP subjects, but PHE preparation should remain centred on the current ePortfolio task, criteria and authentic performance evidence.


### Complete a final evidence audit


Before submission, examine the portfolio as if you know nothing about the student who created it. Can you see the starting point, understand the target, follow the reasoning behind the plan and judge the final result?


Check that every important claim has support. Remove duplicated explanation and material that does not help satisfy the task. Confirm that linked or embedded evidence opens correctly, and never make a last-minute content change without checking whether it affects another section.


You can also revisit[what MYP eAssessment involves](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-myp-eassessment) and[what students should expect from MYP ePortfolio subjects](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-myp-certificate-eportfolio-subjects-and-what-to-expect) before completing your audit.


Good MYP Physical and Health Education revision is a chain of visible decisions. You observe honestly, plan deliberately, practise intelligently and reflect using evidence. RevisionDojo brings that chain together through its Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, Grading tools, Coursework Library and Tutors, making it the ultimate IB resource for turning scattered preparation into a coherent ePortfolio.
